newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Indonesia, Portugal begin Timor talks at U.N.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia, Portugal begin Timor talks at U.N.

text.p: Ambassadorial-level talks between Indonesia and Portugal on the question of East Timor opened on Monday at U.N. headquarters.
The talks, expected to last until Friday, are being chaired by Secretary-General Kofi Annan's special representative for East Timor, Jamsheed Marker, a Pakistani former U.N. ambassador.
Indonesia is represented by its U.N. ambassador, Nugroho Wisnumurti, while Portugal has sent Fernando Neves, its special envoy for East Timor.

After two days of talks at the United Nations in June, the foreign ministers of Portugal and Indonesia agreed that senior officials of the two sides would embark on intensive negotiations on East Timor this summer.

Indonesia occupied East Timor in 1975 after a civil war erupted following Portugal's withdrawal from its colony. In 1976 Indonesia incorporated the territory as its 27th province but this has never been recognised by the United Nations.
U.N.-mediated talks between the foreign minister of Indonesia and Portugal have been continuing since 1983 aimed at finding an internationally acceptable solution to the problem.
After the talks are completed, Marker will travel to South Africa to brief President Nelson Mandela, who has offered to help the United Nations with the long-running dispute.

Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela would discuss with Annan ways to bolster the U.N.'s initiative for peace in East Timor.
"The President is doing everything within the parameters of the U.N. mandate on East Timor. Everything he is doing is designed to underpin the U.N. initiative," he said.
"The President really sees this as a medium to long-term effort. It is not something that can be resolved quickly," he said.
Mankahlana said it was Annan's decision to visit Mandela in person and not to send an envoy, as originally planned.
